title: Rehman Dheri and the question of planned settlement
summary: Rehman Dheri makes early planning visible in streets and blocks, but its ground plan cannot by itself identify the people or institutions that organised the settlement.

body.text: A low mound can contain an unusually legible idea of a town. At Rehman Dheri in the Gomal plain, the arrangement of streets, lanes and blocks is central to the site's importance. The settlement asks a question that is more useful than a contest over which city came first: how much can an ordered plan tell us about the society that made it?

Pakistan's Tentative List description identifies a rectangular, walled settlement whose latest layout remains discernible on the surface and in aerial views. Streets divide the interior into regular blocks. Rain and dew can help reveal buried walls through differences in the ground. This is a plan partly exposed by the condition of the mound, rather than a complete town excavated room by room.
Order before the great cities

Archaeologist Jonathan Mark Kenoyer places Rehman Dheri among the important settlements preceding the mature Indus urban centres. His review of archaeological research highlights the University of Peshawar excavations directed by Farzand Ali Durrani, substantial mud-brick walls, planned streets and early evidence of seals and graffiti. The point is not that urban organisation suddenly appeared at one famous city. Its antecedents can be investigated in several settlements and regional traditions.

A regular street grid implies coordination, but it does not reveal the form of government. The same surviving pattern cannot tell us whether a ruler, a council, neighbouring households or several changing institutions made each decision. Nor does an enclosing wall alone demonstrate a particular war. Planning, authority and defensive intention are related questions, not interchangeable answers.
The surface is only one moment

The Tentative List account also records evidence of craft activity, including kilns and slag, and notes the limitations imposed by comparatively restricted excavation. Surface visibility therefore has a double meaning. It helps make the last settlement arrangement intelligible, while erosion exposes material that once belonged within deposits. A clear photograph can be the result of a damaging process.

Imagine two plans laid over one another: the visible pattern of the final occupation and the sequence of earlier building beneath it. They need not be identical. Establishing continuity requires dated layers, recorded wall relationships and associated finds. A neat aerial outline is an invitation to research, not a substitute for that work.
Making the site accessible without losing evidence

The introduction to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's January 2024 environmental and social management plan treats conservation and visitor development as activities requiring impact assessment and monitoring. It describes a proposed management framework, not proof that every intended intervention has been completed.

That distinction matters for visitors and planners alike. Paths, drainage, signs and protective measures should help people understand the mound without confusing new facilities with ancient remains. Rehman Dheri's strongest story is already in its ground: an early community organised a substantial settlement, and archaeology is still determining how that organisation changed. Respecting the unanswered questions makes the visible order more interesting, not less.

title: Badshahi Mosque and the scale of congregation
summary: Badshahi Mosque turns scale into a sequence of thresholds, open court and covered prayer space. Its authority comes from relationships between these spaces, not dimensions alone.

body.text: Badshahi Mosque is often introduced through numbers: the size of its courtyard, the height of its minarets, the capacity of a congregation. Those measurements express magnitude, but the experience of the building is more precise. Its architecture transforms arrival into a sequence, moving from the surrounding city through an elevated entrance into an open field and finally towards the covered prayer space.

Punjab's Auqaf Department dates Aurangzeb's commission to 1671 and completion to 1673. It places the mosque opposite Lahore Fort, across Hazuri Bagh, and identifies red sandstone and marble inlay among its defining materials. The setting matters as much as the individual façade: mosque, garden and fort can be understood together without treating them as one building or one construction campaign.
A courtyard with direction

The federal archaeological catalogue describes a raised platform, an eastern entrance and a large courtyard before the prayer hall. These elements establish a clear directional relationship. The gateway gathers movement into a threshold; the court releases it into a much wider space; the prayer front gives that openness a destination.

Empty space here is architectural substance. It allows the principal elevations to be seen at a distance and accommodates changing patterns of gathering. An uncrowded photograph can make the court appear purely contemplative, while a large congregation reveals another capacity of the same design. Neither image alone describes its full purpose.

Look at the relationship between the horizontal prayer front and the tall corner minarets. The towers frame the complex at the scale of the city, while repeated openings help the eye read the much longer elevation. Marble accents sharpen the edges and features of the red surface. Authority is produced by the agreement between these scales rather than by ornament applied everywhere with equal intensity.
The building beyond its front

The Department of Archaeology's account describes the interior as a sequence of halls and a central vaulted space. This is a useful correction to the famous frontal view. A mosque is an arrangement of routes, sheltered areas and places of prayer, not merely a picture of domes. Even when access is limited, the exterior should be read as the boundary of inhabited spaces.

Conservation introduces another scale of attention. In its account of work begun in December 2022, the Walled City of Lahore Authority discusses entrance-area and rear-chamber work and roof waterproofing. That dated project description should not be converted into a claim that all work is now finished. It does show why a monumental image depends on less conspicuous tasks, including controlling water at the roof.

Badshahi Mosque remains a religious place as well as a celebrated monument. Observe prayer activity, follow local access instructions and avoid treating worshippers as photographic props. The most rewarding architectural reading combines the long view with the human one: a large composition made meaningful by people moving, pausing and gathering within it.

title: Wazir Khan Mosque: surfaces that reward close looking
summary: Wazir Khan Mosque rewards attention at several distances: a civic presence in the old city, a finely patterned architectural surface and fragile painted work requiring careful documentation.

body.text: Wazir Khan Mosque changes as you approach it. From farther away, its mass and minarets establish a recognisable place in Lahore's old city. Closer to the walls, broad coloured areas resolve into smaller units, inscriptions and floral patterns. Inside, painted surfaces call for a different kind of looking. The building rewards changes in distance rather than one definitive viewpoint.

The Aga Khan Development Network dates its construction to 1634–35 under Hakim Ilmuddin, the governor of Punjab remembered as Wazir Khan. That patronage belongs to the mosque's history, but the surroundings are equally important to its architectural identity. An urban mosque receives people through streets, shops and public space; its threshold is part of a larger inhabited fabric.
Two kinds of surface

The Walled City of Lahore Authority distinguishes the glazed ceramic decoration of the exterior from interior naqqashi wall painting. These should not be flattened into a single category of colourful ornament. Ceramic units and painted plaster have different material properties, assembly methods and conservation needs. Their appearance may be related, but the work that produces and preserves them is not identical.

The Authority also identifies the Calligraphers' Bazaar crossing the entrance axis. This detail complicates the idea of a monument separated from everyday activity. The route to prayer belongs to a setting of exchange and specialised work. Architecture can give public and devotional life adjacent spaces without making them the same activity.
The ground outside matters

AKDN's conservation account explains that accumulated street levels had risen substantially beside the mosque, creating problems at its lower fabric. Its work on the northern façade, completed in 2016, included attention to the adjoining street and former shop spaces. Work around the chowk likewise addressed levels and the relationship between the mosque and its public foreground.

This is a useful way to understand conservation: the decorated wall cannot be treated independently of what touches it. A raised surface can redirect water or conceal a plinth; a repaired façade can remain vulnerable if those conditions persist. The view admired by the visitor depends partly on decisions made at pavement level.
Looking with a record

CyArk documents a 2015 collaboration with Lahore University of Management Sciences that used digital recording and field training at the mosque. Its account describes attention to cracks, frescoes and minaret geometry. These are dated observations used to create a baseline, not a current engineering verdict on every feature.

Documentation also changes the meaning of a detailed photograph. A decorative panel can be recorded for comparison, allowing later observers to distinguish stable variation from material loss. Repeated images from known positions become evidence rather than a succession of attractive impressions.

For a visitor, the practical lesson is simple: look closely without touching, and allow more than one scale of attention. Follow the building from street to gateway, from court to prayer hall, and from overall pattern to individual material. Wazir Khan Mosque's richness emerges through those relationships, not through colour alone.

title: Jahangir’s Tomb at ground level
summary: Jahangir’s tomb is best understood through its low body, shaded circulation and concentrated stonework, with the surrounding Shahdara ensemble extending the story beyond one mausoleum.

body.text: At Jahangir's tomb, it is worth resisting the instinct to look immediately upward. The corner towers draw attention, yet the main building is deliberately low. Its long elevations, sheltered verandah and repeated openings give the monument a strong horizontal character. Much of its architectural interest lies at the level of a person walking around it.

The Walled City of Lahore Authority records Jahangir's death in 1627 and the completion of the mausoleum under Shah Jahan in 1637. It identifies the burial setting as Dilkusha Bagh, associated with Nur Jahan, and describes a square garden organised in the chaharbagh manner. The garden is therefore not a decorative margin around the tomb. It establishes the framework within which the building is approached and understood.
Moving around, moving inward

The federal archaeological description identifies an arcaded verandah before a series of rooms, with vaulted approaches leading towards the central burial chamber. These successive spaces make the transition inward gradual. Open air, shade and enclosed chamber are distinct conditions, each shaping what can be seen and how the visitor moves.

Try reading an elevation as both a surface and an inhabited edge. From the garden, the repeated arches create a measured rhythm. Within the verandah, the same openings become frames for views outward. A façade that appears flat in a photograph is also the boundary of a route.

Red sandstone and light-coloured inlay give that route its visual structure. Pakistan's UNESCO Tentative List description records panel decoration across the exterior and richly worked corner towers. Detail can be followed without assuming that every surviving surface is untouched seventeenth-century fabric. A material history includes repair as well as initial construction.
A small object within a large composition

Inside, the Walled City Authority describes a marble cenotaph marking the grave beneath and bearing floral stone inlay and the attributes of Allah. Distinguishing the memorial above from the burial below avoids a common confusion. The cenotaph concentrates skilled work and remembrance at the centre of a much larger spatial arrangement.

The change in scale is important. Garden paths and building elevations organise movement over considerable distances, while stone joints, coloured inlay and inscriptions ask for slow, close attention. The tomb does not rely on one uninterrupted experience of grandeur; it brings different kinds of attention into sequence.
Shahdara as an ensemble

The Tentative List entry groups Jahangir's tomb with Asif Khan's tomb and Akbari Sarai. The sarai's courtyard, cells and gateways and Asif Khan's domed octagonal mausoleum broaden the architectural comparison. They should not be mistaken for parts of a single tomb, but neither should they disappear from its interpretation.

Seeing these neighbouring structures together reveals differences in enclosure, silhouette and circulation. The low mass of Jahangir's mausoleum becomes more distinctive when it is not treated as a generic Mughal tomb. Begin with the ground-level route, allow the detail to draw you closer, and then return to the larger garden and ensemble. Each scale clarifies the others.

title: Harappa after the excavation trench
summary: Harappa’s archaeology continues after excavation through the study of objects, dates and recorded contexts. Small finds can reveal activities that monumental ruins alone cannot explain.

body.text: An excavation trench is the most visible symbol of archaeology, but it is not where all the important work happens. At Harappa, the interpretation of a small bone tool, a ceramic fragment or a dated deposit can change how an entire settlement is understood. The city survives not only in exposed architecture but also in records and collections that preserve relationships no longer visible on the ground.

The federal archaeological catalogue recalls a damaging episode in the site's modern history: ancient bricks were removed for railway construction in the nineteenth century. It also identifies the excavations begun in 1921. These are different kinds of intervention. One extracted building material; the other attempted to recover evidence. Neither can be understood simply by counting how much ground was disturbed.
A find needs a context

An object removed without a record loses part of its meaning. Its material and shape may remain available for study, but its relationship to a floor, wall, burial or sequence of deposits may be irretrievable. This is why archaeological documentation is not paperwork added after discovery. It is part of the evidence itself.

Kenoyer and Meadow's account of Harappa's Ravi Phase explains how analysis of excavated materials and radiocarbon dates enabled a more detailed settlement chronology. A famous site name therefore covers a changing history, not one undifferentiated moment called the Indus civilisation. Separating phases makes it possible to ask when particular objects, practices and building traditions appeared.
Small tools, substantial questions

The authors illustrate bone points, an awl, polished rib fragments and a perforated piece. They suggest possible connections with basketry, spinning or weaving for some of these objects. The cautious wording matters. A shape can support a functional interpretation without proving one exclusive use.

Such finds redirect attention towards activities that are easily lost in monumental accounts of the past. Producing thread or working fibres requires skill, repeated bodily movements and appropriate tools. The surviving object is only one part of that process. Archaeology must reconstruct the relationship between materials and actions while acknowledging where direct evidence is missing.

A catalogue label should preserve that distinction. “Possible weaving tool” is not a weaker version of a confident but unsupported identification; it is a more accurate description of what is known. Uncertainty can indicate disciplined analysis rather than a failure to reach an answer.
The excavation has a history too

Gregory Possehl's review of research at Harappa describes the multidisciplinary programme undertaken with Pakistan's Department of Archaeology and Museums during the later twentieth century. Different specialists and institutions brought different questions to the same site. Published reports allow those questions, methods and conclusions to be revisited.

For a visitor, the museum and excavation record therefore belong alongside the mounds. Ask where an object was found, how it was dated and which interpretation its evidence actually supports. Harappa becomes richer when it is seen not as a completed picture of an ancient city, but as a place where careful study continues to turn surviving traces into historically meaningful relationships.

title: Derawar Fort and the need for water
summary: Derawar’s powerful walls belong to a desert network sustained by access to water. Reading wells, tanks and routes alongside bastions gives the fort a more complete geography.

body.text: Derawar Fort presents a powerful outline: repeated rounded bastions rising above the flat country of Cholistan. The first impression is defensive, but a fort cannot be understood through walls alone. People occupying it needed water, supplies and connections to routes beyond the enclosure. In this landscape, those less visible requirements are central to the story.

Pakistan's Tentative List submission places Derawar within a wider group of Cholistan forts, rather than presenting it as an isolated desert monument. It relates the network to caravan movement and suggests that access to water helps explain the distribution of fortifications. This is an interpretation of the landscape, not permission to invent a detailed account of every historic journey or garrison.
Looking past the skyline

The Department of Archaeology and Museums records forty bastions, a southern gateway, a well within the fort and a tank outside it. The water features alter the questions a visitor can ask. Where was water available? How did access relate to the enclosure? Which facilities lay inside a defended boundary and which required movement beyond it?

These questions do not require a dramatic siege story. Ordinary occupation would itself have created demands. A wall might control entry, but it could not remove the need for replenishment, maintenance and labour. The fort's apparent self-sufficiency in a distant photograph is therefore misleading: an enclosed building remains connected to a wider environment.

The repeated bastions should also be read as constructed surfaces. The Tentative List account draws attention to patterned brickwork and surviving interior decoration. Defence and visual expression were not necessarily separate concerns. A stronghold could communicate status through the treatment of its walls while accommodating a range of activities within them.
A network, not an empty desert

The UNESCO-hosted submission names other forts including Marotgarh, Maujgarh, Khairgarh and Islamgarh. Their inclusion encourages a regional view. A route has stages; access to resources varies; political boundaries and patterns of occupation change. The most prominent surviving structure cannot by itself stand for all those relationships.

Calling the surroundings empty would also obscure the difference between a lightly built landscape and one without human knowledge. Water sources, paths and seasonal conditions can be significant even where they leave no monumental façade. The fort is a conspicuous element within that geography, not its only meaningful feature.
Keeping the chronology proportionate

The federal catalogue records Sadiq Muhammad Khan's capture of the fort in 1733 while acknowledging uncertainty about earlier history. It is safer to distinguish documented episodes from repeated foundation traditions than to attach a precise ancient date to every visible wall. Repair and rebuilding can substantially change a structure that occupies an older location.

Derawar's value does not depend on settling every uncertain beginning. Its surviving mass, water features and position among other forts already support a compelling account of architecture in a demanding environment. Start with the bastions, but let the well, tank and routes expand the view. The most useful image of the fort includes what sustained it.

title: Hiran Minar: a memorial in a water landscape
summary: Hiran Minar combines an imperial animal memorial with a carefully arranged tank and pavilion. Its landscape is made through water collection, controlled movement and contrasting architectural forms.

body.text: Hiran Minar is more than a tower with a memorable origin story. Near Sheikhupura, the minar stands in relation to a large tank, a central pavilion and the route that connects the pavilion to the bank. Vertical monument, broad water surface and narrow crossing form a composition whose parts make most sense together.

The federal archaeological catalogue associates the tower with Jahangir's memorial to a favoured antelope named Mansraj. That association explains the monument's name and commemorative purpose, but it should not consume the whole visit. The site also offers an unusually clear opportunity to examine the relationship between memory, pleasure architecture and water management.
A tower beside a horizontal landscape

The catalogue describes a tapering brick tower with lime-plastered surfaces and openings that admitted light. Its narrow, rising form contrasts with the tank's broad enclosure. Seen together, the two make scale legible: the tower gives the eye a vertical measure, while the tank establishes distance across the ground.

The UNESCO-hosted Tentative List description records an octagonal pavilion on a platform within the water and a causeway connecting it to a gateway. A crossing like this does more than provide access. It separates the experience of the pavilion from the surrounding bank, making arrival an extended movement through the composition.

Consider the sequence rather than only its reflection in a photograph. A visitor approaches an edge, passes through an architectural threshold and follows a defined route towards a building surrounded by water. The pavilion's position changes the relationship between near and far, centre and boundary. Its apparent simplicity depends on careful spatial decisions.
Water had to reach the tank

The Tentative List account describes a channel from the Aik rivulet and a system for collecting rainwater from the catchment. These features move the interpretation beyond the ornamental. A tank is an engineered receptacle within a larger hydrological setting; its surface does not explain its supply by itself.

Water also makes the monument variable. The appearance of a pavilion, the visibility of edges and the extent of reflections depend on conditions. A particular photograph should not be treated as a permanent specification of the site. Understanding the intended arrangement requires distinguishing built form from a changing water level.
A historic landscape and a future plan

The Urban Unit's published document is explicitly an eco-tourism and restoration master plan with a 2055 horizon. It brings the site into contemporary discussions about access and management, but a proposal is not evidence that every illustrated facility exists. Readers should keep intended interventions separate from the historic elements they are interpreting.

That separation protects the clarity of Hiran Minar's story. The memorial association, the tower's fabric, the tank's supply and the pavilion's approach are connected but different subjects. Giving each its proper scale makes the site more than an anecdote about an emperor's animal: it becomes a landscape in which remembrance and technical organisation were given a deliberate architectural form.

title: Shah Rukn-e-Alam: reading a monumental silhouette
summary: Shah Rukn-e-Alam’s mausoleum combines a powerful octagonal mass with detailed brick, timber and tile work. Its twentieth-century conservation also forms part of the building’s material history.

body.text: The mausoleum of Shah Rukn-e-Alam is immediately recognisable in Multan's skyline, but its silhouette is only the beginning of its architectural character. From a distance, a substantial lower body supports progressively lighter forms and the dome. Close to the building, brickwork, timber and coloured tile divide that mass into a much more intricate construction.

Pakistan's Tentative List submission dates the tomb to the early fourteenth century and associates its construction with Ghiyasuddin Tughluq. The building's significance is not confined to that dynastic attribution. It is also a devotional place and a major work of regional craftsmanship, with a material history that includes substantial modern conservation.
Making a large mass readable

The Department of Archaeology describes an octagonal base with projecting, tapering supports at its angles. Horizontal courses and changes in surface treatment help organise the exterior, while the upper stages lead towards the dome. These features prevent the building from reading as an undifferentiated block.

The octagon is important at both scales. In the overall view, it provides a transition between a broad base and the rounded upper form. At ground level, each face and angle changes the view as a person moves around the building. The monument is not exhausted by a single frontal photograph.

The catalogue also records the relationship of burnt brick and timber framing and the use of brick, tile and wood in the surface articulation. Materials that may appear decorative are part of a more complex assembly. A coloured band can be read visually while also prompting questions about how it was made, fixed and maintained.
Conservation as a chapter of construction

The Aga Khan Award for Architecture's project account describes a major conservation campaign beginning in late 1971 and completed six years later. It included work on foundations and lower brick walls, replacement of lost tiles, repairs to damaged woodwork and treatment of the surrounding site. The surviving monument therefore should not be presented as entirely untouched medieval fabric.

The same account places unusual emphasis on craft training. Experienced practitioners taught thirty-three novices in skills including Multan glazed tile work, wood carving and terracotta. This makes the project more than an episode of structural repair. It linked the care of an existing monument to the transmission of practical knowledge.

That history changes how a visitor might look at a newly regular surface. Repair is not automatically a defect in authenticity, nor is every replacement beyond question. The useful enquiry is what was replaced, why, by whom and with what documentation. A conservation record helps distinguish informed intervention from an invented appearance of age.
From skyline to handwork

Move between the broad and the close view without allowing either to dominate. The dome and tapering body explain why the mausoleum carries such visual weight; joints, bands and worked surfaces reveal the many smaller acts through which that effect was achieved. Shah Rukn-e-Alam's architectural presence belongs to this relationship between monumental form, devotional meaning and continuing skilled care.

title: Bibi Jawindi’s Tomb and the problem of survival
summary: Bibi Jawindi’s partially surviving tomb makes its construction unusually visible. The challenge is to understand and protect that evidence without romanticising loss or confusing repair with recovery.

body.text: The surviving portion of Bibi Jawindi's tomb at Uch can be visually arresting because it is incomplete. The broken enclosure reveals surfaces and structural relationships that a fully intact building would conceal. Yet this visibility comes from loss. An architectural reading should acknowledge the power of the view without treating damage as the monument's ideal condition.

Pakistan's Tentative List submission places the tomb within a group of five monuments at Uch and dates it to around 1494. It describes a broader architectural ensemble associated with religious scholarship and devotional life. Bibi Jawindi's tomb is therefore not a solitary sculptural object in a vacant landscape, even when a tightly framed photograph makes it appear so.
A form assembled in stages

The federal catalogue describes an octagonal base, tapering corner supports and a rising sequence of architectural stages. Recessed arches and bands of glazed decoration articulate the brick surfaces. The large form is legible at a distance, while the tile patterns introduce a much smaller scale of work.

The relationship between the octagon and the upper structure is especially useful to observe. A dome requires a transition from the supporting enclosure beneath it. Where fabric has been lost, the profile can expose something of that construction. This is evidence to study carefully, not an invitation to climb unstable remains for a clearer photograph.

Tile also needs to be understood as material rather than colour alone. Individual pieces belong to a surface attached to a larger wall. If the support moves or moisture affects the assembly, the decorative layer is involved in a structural and environmental problem. A striking blue-and-white pattern does not exist independently of the masonry carrying it.
The history of repair matters

World Monuments Fund's 2000 Watch catalogue discussed the Uch complex as a conservation concern. Its account identified brick laid in earth mortars and warned that some ad hoc cement-based repairs had created problems. That is a dated institutional assessment, not a claim that every condition described remains unchanged today.

The report nevertheless illustrates an enduring question. A repair that looks stronger or more complete can behave differently from the surrounding historic fabric. Compatibility matters alongside appearance. Before judging an intervention by how neatly it fills a gap, ask how it affects the existing structure and whether its purpose and materials are recorded.
More than a picturesque fragment

The UNESCO-hosted description notes that erosion has made aspects of the tombs' profiles and interiors visible. Seeing this clearly requires two ideas at once: a damaged structure can preserve valuable information, and continued damage can destroy that information. Documentation is essential, but it cannot replace the fabric it records.

At Uch, the respectful visitor keeps the individual monument in relation to its neighbouring tombs, mosque and living religious setting. The strongest interpretation neither invents an intact past from imagination nor celebrates the ruin as merely beautiful. It follows the surviving evidence, recognises the work needed for its care and leaves room for the site's continuing significance beyond the photograph.

title: Kot Diji: separating the fort from the archaeological site
summary: Kot Diji names both a Talpur fort and an ancient archaeological settlement. Separating their dates and evidence reveals two different histories that share a landscape, not a single construction story.

body.text: Kot Diji is a place where one name can carry two very different dates. The dramatic hilltop fort belongs to the Talpur period, while the archaeological settlement associated with the same locality reaches back into the development of the Indus civilisation. Confusing them turns a rich landscape into an impossible claim that the standing fortress is thousands of years old.

The distinction is straightforward but important. The federal archaeological catalogue records the fort as a stronghold associated with Mir Sohrab Khan. Sindh's Directorate General of Antiquities separately describes Diji ji Takri, the archaeological mound, and the excavations that helped identify a pre-Harappan cultural phase. These are related through location, not interchangeable historical objects.
Reading the fort on its own terms

The Department of Archaeology describes a steep approach, successive gateways and terraces, stone construction and projecting bastions. Those features belong to a defensive architectural sequence. An entrance is not simply a hole in the outer wall: the approach itself can organise and constrain movement before a person reaches the interior.

Pakistan's March 2026 Tentative List submission places the fort in the late-eighteenth-century Talpur context. That is a nomination-stage record, not inscription on the World Heritage List. The document contains differing precise construction dates, so a broad period is more responsible here than false certainty about a single year.

The fort's height allows the surrounding landscape to become part of its interpretation. Visibility, approach and the placement of enclosure walls are useful observations. They do not require claims that the fort was literally impregnable or that its defences were never tested. Architectural capacity and documented military events are different kinds of evidence.
Reading the mound differently

At the archaeological site, the evidence works through deposits and objects rather than standing Talpur walls. Sindh's Antiquities account explains that excavation recovered a sequence of occupation, mud-brick building and distinctive pottery. These findings contributed to understanding developments preceding the mature Harappan cities.

An archaeological culture is a scholarly way of describing recurring material characteristics; it is not automatically the name an ancient population used for itself. Likewise, shared pottery forms do not prove that all people using them belonged to one political state. The value of the Kot Diji evidence lies in making comparisons and changes investigable, not in supplying an effortless identity label.
Two histories in one visit

The fort and the mound invite different questions. At the fort, examine approach, elevation, masonry and enclosure. At the archaeological settlement, ask how deposits were recorded, which materials distinguish phases and how conclusions depend on excavated context. Neither method can simply be transferred to the other.

Keeping the two histories distinct does not make the landscape fragmented. It reveals how a locality can acquire significance at widely separated times and for different reasons. The strongest account of Kot Diji holds both stories together while preserving the distance between them: an ancient settlement important to archaeological research, and a much later fortress expressing Talpur power through the control of a prominent site.
